newsitem.title: CHINA: HK cabinet mulls deporting child migrants to China.
newsitem.headline: HK cabinet mulls deporting child migrants to China.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa convened his first post-handover cabinet meeting on Tuesday and was reported considering a law to deport hundreds of children back to China as illegal migrants
Tung's Executive Council held its first session since London handed the 156-year-old British colony back to China a week ago.
Under the handover treaty Hong Kong remains a capitalist society with great autonomy, and China is keeping it sealed off from the rest of the country as a special region.
No official agenda was released in advance, but political sources have said the kitchen cabinet will consider immigration, labour and electoral problems.

The English-language South China Morning Post newspaper, quoting unnamed sources, said Tung would be asked to rush through a bill allowing children to be deported despite a claim to residency in Hong Kong.
The bill would be retroactive to July 1, the day Hong Kong became a Chinese special region, it said.
Hong Kong has been inundated with young illegal migrants from the Chinese mainland over the past year.
They typically have a parent legally resident in Hong Kong and would themselves have a right of abode under Hong Kong's post-handover constitution.

But a long wait, because of a huge backlog of an estimated 60,000 cases in China awaiting clearance to move to Hong Kong, has driven many families to smuggle in the children, violating frontier regulations.
Last week hundreds of families, who had been hiding smuggled children, turned in their infants to immigration authorities, believing the new government would not deport them.
But Tung is under political pressure from legislators and advisers to carry through the deportations and force the families to apply for immigration through legal channels.
Otherwise, they argue, liberal precedent might unleash a flood of further smuggling attempts.
"Because of the extent of the problem, it is necessary for us to pass the laws as quickly as possible," said Liberal Party leader Allen Lee. "The longer we delay, the bigger the problem will be."
If approved, the bill could go before the legislature on Wednesday.
